\chapter{Two Thoughts, One Sentence}
\label{ch:ge-verbindungen}
\hlchaptermodality{48}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can join two thoughts with and, or, but, but-rather and because, and I know which of them sends the verb to the end.}

Every verb the book owns is given a reason, twice: once with denn and the verb in slot two, once with weil and the verb walked to the far end. The chapter is where the reader learns that German saves its last position for the piece that completes the sense -- the third time the book has sent something there, after the separable prefix and the nicht that cancels a verb.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[oder]{oder — \textquotedblleft{}or,\textquotedblright{} and the question every German ends with}

\label{lesson:GE-C35-oder}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Und} has been yours since the wellbeing lessons and is the only joining word in the book. Say \textquotedblleft{}Kaffee und Tee\textquotedblright{}, then take the second one.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} two chapters back, the two shapes of \emph{how many} — \emph{wie viel} for what you cannot count, \emph{wie viele} for what you can
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: oder}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{oder} — \textquotedblleft{}or\textquotedblright{}.
\end{quote}

Said \emph{OH-der}, long \emph{o}, soft trailing \emph{r}.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Kaffee oder Tee?} · \textbf{Milch oder Wasser?}
\end{quote}

Nothing moves around it. Like \emph{und}, it stands between two things and joins them, and the verb stays where it was.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{oder} and English \textbf{or} are the same Germanic word, \emph{\textbf{*efþau}} — English wore it to one syllable, German kept two. German then gave it a job English builds a whole clause for. Put \textbf{oder?} on the end of a statement:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Das ist gut, oder?} — \textquotedblleft{}That's good, isn't it?\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

English needs \emph{isn't it}, \emph{doesn't he}, \emph{haven't they} — a different tag for every verb and person. German needs one word, unchanged. You will hear it constantly.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Kaffee oder Tee?\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}Milch oder Wasser?\textquotedblright{}
  \item the animals — \textquotedblleft{}Hund oder Katze?\textquotedblright{}
  \item both joiners in one breath — \textquotedblleft{}Brot und Wein\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}Brot oder Wein\textquotedblright{}
  \item the tag — \textquotedblleft{}Das ist gut, oder?\textquotedblright{}
  \item a choice with a quantity in it — \textquotedblleft{}Wie viel Kaffee oder wie viel Tee?\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}Wie viele Hunde oder wie viele Katzen?\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}Kaffee oder Tee? — Das ist gut, oder?\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}coffee or tea\textquotedblright{}. What English word is \emph{oder}? (\emph{\textbf{Or}}, the same word with a syllable worn off.) What does \emph{oder?} do at the end of a sentence? (\textbf{Turns it into a question expecting agreement} — English's \emph{isn't it}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[aber]{aber — \textquotedblleft{}but,\textquotedblright{} the word that turns a sentence around}

\label{lesson:GE-C35-aber}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Und} adds. \emph{Oder} offers a choice. Neither can say that the second half disagrees with the first.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: aber}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{aber} — \textquotedblleft{}but\textquotedblright{}.
\end{quote}

Said \emph{AH-ber}, long \emph{a}, soft \emph{r}.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Der Tag ist gut, aber ich bin müde.} — \textquotedblleft{}The day is good, but I'm tired.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Das ist schön, aber teuer.} — \textquotedblleft{}That's lovely, but expensive.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

The verb does not move. \emph{Aber} joins two whole sentences without disturbing either — which is what makes it, \emph{und} and \emph{oder} one family, and worth knowing before the two words in this chapter that \textbf{do} disturb things.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{aber} was once \emph{\textbf{*afar}}, \textquotedblleft{}after, again\textquotedblright{} — a cousin of German \textbf{ab} (\textquotedblleft{}off\textquotedblright{}) and of Greek \textbf{apo-}, which English carries in \emph{apostrophe} and \emph{apology}. A word about position became a word about contrast.

English did the identical thing with different pieces. \textbf{But} is Old English \emph{\textbf{be-ūtan}}, \textquotedblleft{}by-out\textquotedblright{} — \emph{without}, \emph{outside of}. Two languages, two small words about where a thing stands, both promoted to mean \emph{however}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Der Tag ist gut, aber ich bin müde.\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Das ist schön, aber ich habe keine Zeit.\textquotedblright{}
  \item with last chapter's negative — \textquotedblleft{}Ich habe Tee, aber keinen Kaffee.\textquotedblright{}
  \item the three joiners in a row — \textquotedblleft{}und, oder, aber\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}Der Tag ist gut, aber ich bin müde.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say the three joiners you now own. (\emph{\textbf{Und, oder, aber}}.) Does the verb move after any of them? (\textbf{No.}) What did \emph{aber} mean before it meant \textquotedblleft{}but\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{After, again} — a word about position.) Next: the fourth \textquotedblleft{}but\textquotedblright{}, which German keeps for one job only.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[sondern]{sondern — the \textquotedblleft{}but\textquotedblright{} that corrects}

\label{lesson:GE-C35-sondern}



\begin{quote}
German already has one word that exists only to contradict a negative: \textbf{doch}, which answers \emph{\textquotedblleft{}Hast du keinen Hund?\textquotedblright{}} with \emph{yes I do}. It has a second, and it does the same job inside a sentence.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: sondern}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{sondern} — \textquotedblleft{}but rather\textquotedblright{}, after a negative, when the second half \textbf{replaces} what the first half denied.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Das ist nicht schwarz, sondern weiß.} — \textquotedblleft{}That isn't black, it's white.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Compare it with the word from the last lesson, which cannot do this job:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Das ist schwarz, aber schön.} — two things, both true. \textbf{Das ist nicht schwarz, sondern weiß.} — the second corrects the first.
\end{quote}

The test is short: if the first half is negative and the second half puts something in its place, German wants \emph{sondern}. Otherwise it wants \emph{aber}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{sondern} is also a verb, meaning \textbf{to separate}, and English keeps that verb too: \textbf{sunder}, and the \emph{asunder} of \emph{torn asunder}. So the joiner that corrects a negative is, underneath, the word for keeping two things apart — which is exactly what it does to the wrong answer and the right one.

English has no separate word here and never did. It says \emph{but} both times and lets the tone do the work. German marks the difference, and it marks it a second time with \textbf{doch} in answers, so the pattern is one you have already met.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Decide which \textquotedblleft{}but\textquotedblright{} the sentence wants before you say it.

Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item a correction — \textquotedblleft{}Das ist nicht schwarz, sondern weiß.\textquotedblright{}
  \item a correction — \textquotedblleft{}Das ist kein Kaffee, sondern Tee.\textquotedblright{}
  \item two things both true, so \emph{aber} — \textquotedblleft{}Der Wein ist rot, aber gut.\textquotedblright{}
  \item the answer-word that does the same job — \textquotedblleft{}Doch!\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}Das ist nicht schwarz, sondern weiß.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
When does German want \emph{sondern} rather than \emph{aber}? (\textbf{After a negative, when the second half replaces what was denied.}) What English verb is \emph{sondern}? (\textbf{To sunder} — to separate.) Which answer-word does the same job in one syllable? (\emph{\textbf{Doch}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[denn]{denn — \textquotedblleft{}because,\textquotedblright{} with nothing moved}

\label{lesson:GE-C35-denn}



\begin{quote}
Four joiners are yours and none of them can give a reason. Say the four, and note that the verb has stayed in slot two after every one of them.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: denn}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{denn} — \textquotedblleft{}for\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}because\textquotedblright{}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Ich bin müde, denn ich habe nicht geschlafen.} — \textquotedblleft{}I'm tired, because I didn't sleep.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Look at the second half. \textbf{Ich} first, \textbf{habe} second — the ordinary order the book has used since your first question. \emph{Denn} gives a reason and changes nothing, which makes it the easiest reason-word German has and the one to reach for first.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{denn} and \textbf{dann} (\textquotedblleft{}then\textquotedblright{}) were one word. German split the pair and gave each half a job: \emph{dann} says \textbf{when}, \emph{denn} says \textbf{why}. English is a cousin of both and kept only the \emph{when} — \textbf{then} — so the \emph{why} half has no English survivor at all.

You can still hear the join. \emph{\textquotedblleft{}It rained, then I stayed home\textquotedblright{}} and \emph{\textquotedblleft{}It rained, so I stayed home\textquotedblright{}} are nearly the same sentence, and a reason is very often a \emph{before} wearing different clothes.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Ich bin müde, denn ich habe keine Zeit.\textquotedblright{}
  \item with the past you already own — \textquotedblleft{}Ich bin müde, denn ich habe gelernt.\textquotedblright{}
  \item all five joiners — \textquotedblleft{}und, oder, aber, sondern, denn\textquotedblright{}
  \item prove the verb has not moved — \textquotedblleft{}denn ich habe …\textquotedblright{}, subject first, verb second
  \item the question this word answers — \textquotedblleft{}Warum?\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}…, denn ich habe keine Zeit.\textquotedblright{}
  \item the other two W-words, each answered with \emph{denn} — \textquotedblleft{}Wer lernt Deutsch?\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}Wann lernst du?\textquotedblright{}, and their English twins, \emph{who} and \emph{when}, which begin with the \emph{wh-} Grimm's law left behind
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}Ich bin müde, denn ich habe gelernt.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where does the verb stand after \emph{denn}? (\textbf{Second, as always.}) What word was \emph{denn} once the same as? (\emph{\textbf{Dann}}, \textquotedblleft{}then\textquotedblright{} — English kept only that half.) Next: the other word for \textquotedblleft{}because\textquotedblright{}, which does not leave the sentence alone.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[weil]{weil — \textquotedblleft{}because,\textquotedblright{} and the verb goes to the end}

\label{lesson:GE-C35-weil}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Denn} gave a reason and moved nothing. This word gives the same reason and moves the most important thing in the sentence.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} two chapters back, the phrase that says a thing exists — \emph{es gibt}, and the marked form it demands
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: weil}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{weil} — \textquotedblleft{}because\textquotedblright{}.
\end{quote}

Said \emph{vile}, rhyming with \emph{mile}: the same \emph{ei} you say in \emph{kein} and \emph{nein}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the verb travels to the far end}]
\begin{quote}
After \textbf{weil}, the verb leaves slot two and goes \textbf{last}.
\end{quote}

Set the two reason-words side by side and only one thing differs:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Ich bin müde, denn ich }habe\textbf{ keine Zeit.} \textbf{Ich bin müde, weil ich keine Zeit }habe\textbf{.}
\end{quote}

Same words, same meaning, and \emph{habe} has walked to the end of the line.

This is the third time the book has sent something to the far end of a German sentence. A separable prefix goes there. \emph{Nicht} goes there when it cancels the verb. Now the verb itself goes there, whenever a word like \emph{weil} opens the clause. German saves its last position for the piece that completes the sense, and it is worth expecting from here on.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{weil} is a worn-down \textbf{dieweil}, \textquotedblleft{}during the while that\textquotedblright{} — and \textbf{die Weile} is English \textbf{while}, the same word. So German's \emph{because} began as a word about \textbf{time}.

English walked the same road with \textbf{since}: \emph{\textquotedblleft{}since Tuesday\textquotedblright{}} is time, \emph{\textquotedblleft{}since you asked\textquotedblright{}} is cause, and nobody notices the crossing. A reason and a before-and-after are close enough that both languages made the trip.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say the \emph{denn} version first, then move the verb.

Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}…, denn ich habe keine Zeit.\textquotedblright{} $\to$ \textquotedblleft{}…, weil ich keine Zeit habe.\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Ich lerne Deutsch, weil ich in Berlin wohne.\textquotedblright{}
  \item the verb travelling, out loud — \textquotedblleft{}habe … keine Zeit habe\textquotedblright{}
  \item the three things German sends to the end — a prefix, \emph{nicht}, and now the verb
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}Ich bin müde, weil ich keine Zeit habe.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What happens to the verb after \emph{weil}? (\textbf{It goes to the end.}) And after \emph{denn}? (\textbf{Nothing} — it stays in slot two.) What word is hiding inside \emph{weil}? (\textbf{Die Weile} — English \emph{while}.) Which English reason-word made the same journey from time to cause? (\emph{\textbf{Since}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Zwei Gedanken — the chapter, run cold}

\label{lesson:GE-R35-zwei-gedanken}



\begin{quote}
Six joiners. Five leave the verb where it stands and one does not. Name all six, then name the one that moves it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn: joining, without moving anything}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item joined — \textquotedblleft{}Brot und Wein\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}Kaffee oder Tee\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}Milch oder Wasser\textquotedblright{}
  \item contrasted — \textquotedblleft{}Der Wein ist rot, aber gut.\textquotedblright{}
  \item corrected — \textquotedblleft{}Das ist nicht weiß, sondern schwarz.\textquotedblright{}
  \item the six colours, two of them corrections — \textquotedblleft{}Nicht grün, sondern gelb. Nicht blau, sondern rot.\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Your turn: the distant band — reasons over everything}
Every verb the book owns can now carry a reason. Say each pair twice — once with \emph{denn} and the verb in place, once with \emph{weil} and the verb at the end.

Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Ich lerne Deutsch, denn ich wohne in Berlin.\textquotedblright{} $\to$ \textquotedblleft{}…, weil ich in Berlin wohne.\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Ich bin müde, denn ich habe keine Zeit.\textquotedblright{} $\to$ \textquotedblleft{}…, weil ich keine Zeit habe.\textquotedblright{}
  \item the verbs of taking in and putting out, each given a reason — \emph{lesen, schreiben, hören, sehen}
  \item the verbs of the body — \emph{schlafen, sitzen, stehen, gehen, laufen, rennen}
  \item the pair with a prefix that already goes to the end — \emph{öffnen} and \emph{schließen}
  \item the three things German sends last — a prefix, \emph{nicht}, the verb after \emph{weil}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which joiner corrects a negative? (\emph{\textbf{Sondern}}.) Which two give a reason, and what is the difference? (\emph{\textbf{Denn}}, verb in slot two; \emph{\textbf{weil}}, verb at the end.) Which of the six is also a tag question? (\emph{\textbf{Oder?}}) And which one is \emph{die Weile} in disguise? (\emph{\textbf{Weil}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
